ABSTRACT: Confinement of hydrocarbons in nanoscale pockets and pores provides tunable capability for controlling molecules in catalysts, sorbents, and membranes for reaction and separation applications. While computation of the enthalpic interactions of hydrocarbons in confined spaces has improved, understanding and predicting the entropy of confined molecules remains a challenge. Here we show, using a set of nine aluminosilicate zeolite frameworks with broad variation in pore and cavity structure, that the entropy of adsorption can be predicted as a linear combination of rotational and translational entropy. The extent of entropy lost upon adsorption is predicted using only a single material descriptor, the occupiable volume ( $ V_{occ} $). Predictive capability of confined molecular entropy permits an understanding of the relation with adsorption enthalpy, the ability to computationally screen microporous materials, and an understanding of the role of confinement on the kinetics of molecules in confined spaces.

On the basis of this shape-selective feature , highly effective molecular separations and selective catalytic conversions can be achieved within zeolitic structures that are difficult to accomplish with other materials and/or techniques . $ ^ { 1-3 } $ So far, several shape-selectivity mechanisms have been elucidated and applications identified. $ ^{2-18} $ In common molecular sieving, bulky molecules adsorb preferentially over bulkier species as a result of steric constraints imposed by the zeolites' framework, e.g., linear alkane molecules compared to branched isomers. $ ^{19-23} $ Besides this common adsorption competition based on molecular bulkiness, the reverse phenomenon can also occur, i.e., competitive adsorption in favor of the bulkier species. Experiments revealed preferential adsorption of branched alkanes over their linear isomers on specific zeolites with tubular pore systems such as SAPO-5 and Mordenite. $ ^{24-28} $ Molecular simulations indicated that in such zeolites, depending on conditions, branched alkanes are preferentially adsorbed at the expense of linear isomers. $ ^{29-34} $ The present manuscript discusses the mechanisms of shape selectivity in n- and isoalkane adsorption on zeolite MCM-22. This zeolite with IZA code MWW is a relatively new synthetic material that has an unusual and quite complex pore structure. $ ^{35} $ Its framework is composed of two independent pore systems. The enthalpy and the entropy contributions to the Gibbs free energies were calculated at T = 298 K and partial pressure of 1 atm (101325 Pa). The enthalpy (H) of gas-phase pyridine and acetonitrile molecules is defined as the sum of total electronic energy ( $ E_{el} $), internal vibrational energy ( $ E_{v} $), zero-point vibrational energy (ZPVE), as well as the rotational and translational contributions to the internal energy: $ H = E_{el} + E_{v} + ZPVE + E_{R} + E_{t} $. The corresponding calculated entropies (S) includes translational, ( $ S_{t} $) vibrational, ( $ S_{v} $) and rotational ( $ S_{r} $) degrees of freedom: $ S = S_{t} + S_{v} + S_{r} $. All the considered systems are in singlet state, thus the electronic contribution to the entropy is zero. Since both adsorbed molecules are constrained in the zeolite cavity their entropy contributions in the adsorption complexes were corrected as follows: the translational and rotational degrees of freedom were reduced by 1 and 1.28 [37]. The Gibbs free energies of the zeolite support consist of only vibrational and electronic contributions. The expressions of all enthalpy and entropy contributions can be found in Ref. [38].

The first attempts to describe guest-induced flexibility in zeolites were done using molecular dynamics simulations. $ ^{79-82} $ Rigid zeolitic force fields were dynamically modified using transition state theory to include lattice flexibility, and the results obtained by these models were in good agreement with experimental data. $ ^{79-81,83,84} $ It was shown that framework flexibility in silicalite-1 (MFI-type framework) is responsible for the adsorption of large molecules such as isobutane and heptane with inflection behavior at high loadings, $ ^{80} $ while enhanced self-diffusivity at low loadings of short alkanes (i.e. methane and n-butane) was observed. $ ^{81} $ Framework flexibility is also crucial for aromatics adsorption on MFI zeolite, especially at high pressures. $ ^{84,85} $ While the use of rigid zeolitic models led to the underestimation of the aromatics adsorption in MFI zeolite by a factor of two, $ ^{84,85} $ the use of flexible models to simulate diffusion coefficients of various alkanes in silicalite-1 zeolite resulted in a convergence of experimental and theoretical values. $ ^{86} $ Recently by using in situ integrated differential phase contrast scanning transmission electron microscopy (iDPC-STEM) while adsorbing benzene molecules on MFI zeolite, Xiong et al. showed that the MFI structure goes through severe deformations giving another proof of guest-induced flexibility in zeolites (see Fig. 4). $ ^{87} $

2.4.4. Trapdoor. Traditional diﬀusion models primarily consider two types of interactions: those between guest molecules (guest–guest) and those between guest molecules and the zeolite framework (guest–host). However, when cations are present in the zeolite structure, a third interaction—involving guest molecules, the framework, and cations (guest–host-cation)—must also be accounted for. A striking example of such ternary interactions is the well-known ‘‘molecular trapdoor’’. This phenomenon, also referred to as the ‘‘gating effect’’, describes a unique molecular sieving mechanism in certain zeolites and related porous materi- als. Here, extra-framework cations function as dynamic gate- keepers at pore apertures, selectively controlling molecular diffusion to achieve highly discriminative adsorption and separation.9,147,187 To date, ‘‘trapdoor’’ has been observed in several zeolites, including RHO (DNL-6),188–190 CHA (SAPO-34, SSZ-13),147,191,192 MWF (ZSM-25),149,193 HEU (Clinoptilolite),194

The turnover rates of olefin formation during cyclohexanol (CyOH) dehydration within the autoclave reactor initially increase with the local ionic strength within a micropore, and further decrease along ionic strength promotion, shown as a volcano-shaped dependence of TOFs on the ionic strength of zeolites. In the following appendix , we derive the entropy of adsorption in the case of infinite dilution and show how it may be related to familiar thermodynamic quantities ( cf . eq 5 ) . To begin , we define our adsorption entropy in the limit of infinite dilution via

$$ \Delta s_{\mathrm{ads}}^{\infty}=\lim_{N/V\rightarrow0}\left[\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{ads}}-\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{gas}}\right] $$

$$ =S_{ads}(N=1,V,T)-S_{gas}(N=1,V,T) $$

where the subscripts “ads” and “gas” labels identify the adsorbed (confined) and gas (bulk) phases, respectively. Given the constraints of a fixed number of molecules (N), volume (V), and temperature (T), it is natural to continue working in the canonical ensemble. (As in the main text, lowercase symbols identify intensive molecular or molar properties, whereas the uppercase indicates an extensive property.) For the molecules that we examine in this work (e.g., rigid molecules with no internal degrees of freedom), the canonical partition function Q may be expressed as

$$ \begin{aligned}Q(N,V,T)&=Q_{trans}(N,V,T)Q_{rot}(N,V,T)\\&\quad\times Z(N,V,T)\end{aligned} $$

where $ Q_{trans} $ and $ Q_{rot} $ are the translational and rotational partition functions (which are unaffected by confinement) and Z is the configurational partition function. The translational and rotational partition functions are available in the usual statistical mechanics texts $ ^{44,45} $ but are ultimately unimportant for the derivation that follows.

descriptor_candidates.name: conf_ratio_tightness
descriptor_candidates.formula: Vol / (AV * density * Vol + 1) + AV / (AV + Vol * density) * 0 + (AV / (AV + Vol * density))**1
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss (per R) increases monotonically with the framework-to-accessible volume packing ratio (packing tightness), so a descriptor combining AV, Vol and density in the source numerical scale predicts s_ads/s_gas better than AV alone, because tighter packing restricts both translational and rotational freedom. Falsified if MAE(entropy loss/R) of the full 14-input network is not reduced by adding this descriptor, or if the coefficient of the descriptor has the wrong sign.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E02: occupiable volume is a strong single descriptor of confined entropy; packing tightness (inverse free volume per framework volume) captures confinement strength beyond raw pore volume. Source evidence: E02. This re-expresses existing inputs and is a new_combination, not a new discovery.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Hold-out MAE of entropy loss/R with this descriptor added to the 14-input network must be lower than the baseline MAE; otherwise rejected.

descriptor_candidates.name: shape_aniso_confinement
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Molecular shape anisotropy (asphericity from principal moments and SPAN/PBF aspect) modulates entropy loss: rod-like anisotropic molecules lose more rotational entropy in one-dimensional channels (TON/MOR-like regimes) and less in large-cage frameworks (FAU-like regimes). Adding this molecular-aspect descriptor to the network lowers MAE of entropy loss/R specifically for the subset of long narrow-pore systems.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E01 (molecule-shape/confinement coupling of ΔS_conf) and E04 (shape selectivity): rotational freedom loss depends on the match between molecular aspect ratio and pore dimensionality. PMI1/PMI3 and SPAN/PBF encode asphericity. Source evidence: E01, E04; the descriptor combination is inference.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Stratified evaluation: descriptor must reduce MAE on anisotropic-molecule/1D-channel subsets without degrading global MAE; if global MAE increases or subset improvement is absent, hypothesis is rejected.

descriptor_candidates.name: window_size_mismatch
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss grows with (i) the mismatch between periodic and probe-accessible limiting pore dimensions (narrow windows vs. larger cages create rotational traps) and (ii) the ratio of accessible surface area measures (geometric roughness of the confinement surface). The combined descriptor improves MAE of entropy loss/R beyond the baseline 14 inputs, with the largest gains for cage-window frameworks.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E09 (configurational partition function governs adsorption entropy) and E06 (framework flexibility/window gating alters confined mobility): window–cage size mismatch restricts rotational and positional sampling of adsorbates. Source evidence: E09, E06; the descriptor is inference.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Ablation: adding this descriptor must reduce hold-out MAE of entropy loss/R relative to the 14-input baseline, and its fitted sign must correspond to increased entropy loss with mismatch; sign reversal or no MAE reduction falsifies the hypothesis.

descriptor_candidates.name: surface_to_size_coupling
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss per R increases with the ratio of accessible molecular surface to its characteristic geometric size (surface-to-volume-coupling), scaled by the material-level surface density term ASA/Vol; molecules presenting large contactable surface relative to their size in frameworks with high specific surface lose more translational entropy via multi-wall contact. Adding this descriptor reduces hold-out MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.546 R (current best after round 2).
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference: configurational partition function (E09) shrinks with the fraction of configurational space excluded by walls; a high surface-to-size ratio means the adsorbate interacts with confinement on many degrees of freedom simultaneously, whereas E02 shows occupiable volume alone captures only part of this effect. Source evidence: E02, E09; the coupling of molecular-surface and framework-specific-surface scales is inference.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Hold-out MAE of entropy loss/R with this descriptor added to the 14-input network must be lower than the baseline 14-input MAE; if MAE is unchanged or increases, or the fitted association indicates reduced entropy loss with higher surface-to-size ratio, the hypothesis is rejected.

descriptor_candidates.name: compactness_confinement
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss grows with molecular compactness (volume relative to the cube of its maximum span dimension PBF) times framework tightness (pore volume fraction AV at source density scale): compact, near-spherical molecules in tight frameworks retain more rotational entropy than expected from volume alone, while elongated molecules in tight frameworks lose more. The interaction of molecular compactness with framework packing therefore improves MAE of entropy loss/R over the baseline, especially for small gases in narrow-pore frameworks.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E01 (molecule-shape/confinement coupling in ΔS_conf remains undetermined) and E09 (rotational partition function enters the canonical partition function but confinement acts through the configurational term): compactness measures how much rotational phase space survives at fixed occupiable volume. Source evidence: E01, E09; the compactness-times-porosity product is inference.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Adding the descriptor must reduce hold-out MAE of entropy loss/R relative to the 14-input baseline; a stratified check should show the largest error reduction on compact-molecule/tight-framework systems. If global MAE rises or improvement is absent on all strata, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: aspect_window_fit
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss increases when the molecular middle-to-minimum principal-moment aspect ratio is high and the framework limiting diameter (lsd_f) is small relative to the probe-accessible dimension (lsd_p), because molecules elongated in two dimensions must orient precisely to pass through and rattle within windows (orientation-restricted configurational entropy). The SPAN/lsd_p term captures steric overcrowding relative to the aperture. Adding this descriptor lowers MAE of entropy loss/R below the round-2 best of 0.546 R, with gains concentrated on 1D-channel and window-cage frameworks.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E04 (shape matching between molecule and pore produces distinct adsorption states) and E10 (molecules penetrate pores slightly smaller than their free size only via framework/molecular distortion, implying entropic cost of squeezed passage); E09 locates the effect in the configurational partition function. Source evidence: E04, E09, E10; the specific aspect-to-window fitting product is inference.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Hold-out MAE of entropy loss/R must decrease relative to the baseline and to the retained window_size_mismatch descriptor's residuals; if the descriptor fails to reduce MAE or only duplicates the retained descriptor's contribution (no residual variance explained), the hypothesis is rejected.

descriptor_candidates.name: window_asphere_trap
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss per R increases when molecular asphericity (PMI3/PMI2, SPAN) is large AND the framework limiting diameter is small relative to the probe-accessible dimension, because elongated or two-dimensionally extended molecules must adopt narrow orientation distributions to pass through and rattle within windows. Adding this descriptor reduces hold-out MAE of entropy loss/R below the current best 0.546 R, with gains concentrated on window-cage and 1D-channel frameworks.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference: E09 locates adsorption entropy loss in the configurational partition function, whose volume shrinks with orientational constraints; E04/E10 indicate shape matching and squeezed passage through windows carry entropic cost. The product of molecular asphericity and window-to-cage dimension ratio encodes the number of orientation degrees of freedom removed at the bottleneck; it is distinct from the retained descriptor, which uses only lsd mismatch and surface ratios.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Adding the descriptor to the 14-input network must lower hold-out MAE of entropy loss/R versus 0.546 R, and must explain residual variance beyond window_size_mismatch (ablation check); MAE increase or pure duplication of the retained descriptor's contribution falsifies the hypothesis.

descriptor_candidates.name: free_path_packing
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss grows with the ratio of molecular dimension to probe-accessible pore dimension (translational freezing when the molecule barely fits the free path) modulated by the remaining free-volume fraction (1 - AV*density/(AV*density+1)) and by the molecular surface roughness term. This coupling of molecular size to pore free-path and residual free volume improves MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.546 R, with the largest gains for tight small-pore frameworks.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference: E02 shows occupiable volume alone predicts much of the entropy loss but not all; E09 attributes the remainder to the configurational partition function. When the molecular cube-root size approaches the accessible pore dimension, translation collapses to hopping between cages, and the surviving free-volume fraction (from AV at the source density scale) determines how many configurational states remain. The roughness term captures multi-wall contact (inference, not a literature relation).
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Hold-out MAE of entropy loss/R with this descriptor added must be below the 0.546 R baseline; if MAE is unchanged or worse, or the fitted sign corresponds to reduced entropy loss at small free paths, the hypothesis is rejected.

descriptor_candidates.name: moment_doorway_index
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss is largest when the discrepancy between a normalized molecular inertial bulk (PMI3/Vol^2) and a normalized doorway measure (lsd_f relative to the combined limiting dimension) is large, scaled by mass per contact area (MW/LabuteASA): heavy, compact molecules squeezed through relatively small doorways lose rotational entropy disproportionately because their inertial resistance prevents the framework-assisted distortion allowed for light molecules (E10). Adding this mismatch-of-normalized-bulks descriptor lowers MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.546 R.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference: E10 reports that molecules penetrate pores smaller than their free size only via molecular/framework distortion, an entropic cost that should scale with mass per surface (inertia vs. contact). E09 places the effect in the configurational term. The descriptor compares a molecular normalized bulk against a framework normalized doorway so the network can learn a threshold-like fitting regime; neither factor alone is claimed as new, only their normalized mismatch.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Hold-out MAE of entropy loss/R must drop below 0.546 R when this descriptor is added, and the improvement must persist in the subgroup with high MW/(LabuteASA+1); absence of improvement, global MAE increase, or a fitted sign indicating reduced entropy loss for large doorway mismatch falsifies the hypothesis.

candidates.name: window_asphere_trap
candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss per R increases when molecular asphericity (PMI3/PMI2, SPAN) is large AND the framework limiting diameter is small relative to the probe-accessible dimension, because elongated or two-dimensionally extended molecules must adopt narrow orientation distributions to pass through and rattle within windows. Adding this descriptor reduces hold-out MAE of entropy loss/R below the current best 0.546 R, with gains concentrated on window-cage and 1D-channel frameworks.
candidates.rationale: Inference: E09 locates adsorption entropy loss in the configurational partition function, whose volume shrinks with orientational constraints; E04/E10 indicate shape matching and squeezed passage through windows carry entropic cost. The product of molecular asphericity and window-to-cage dimension ratio encodes the number of orientation degrees of freedom removed at the bottleneck; it is distinct from the retained descriptor, which uses only lsd mismatch and surface ratios.
candidates.falsification_criteria: Adding the descriptor to the 14-input network must lower hold-out MAE of entropy loss/R versus 0.546 R, and must explain residual variance beyond window_size_mismatch (ablation check); MAE increase or pure duplication of the retained descriptor's contribution falsifies the hypothesis.

candidates.name: free_path_packing
candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss grows with the ratio of molecular dimension to probe-accessible pore dimension (translational freezing when the molecule barely fits the free path) modulated by the remaining free-volume fraction (1 - AV*density/(AV*density+1)) and by the molecular surface roughness term. This coupling of molecular size to pore free-path and residual free volume improves MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.546 R, with the largest gains for tight small-pore frameworks.
candidates.rationale: Inference: E02 shows occupiable volume alone predicts much of the entropy loss but not all; E09 attributes the remainder to the configurational partition function. When the molecular cube-root size approaches the accessible pore dimension, translation collapses to hopping between cages, and the surviving free-volume fraction (from AV at the source density scale) determines how many configurational states remain. The roughness term captures multi-wall contact (inference, not a literature relation).
candidates.falsification_criteria: Hold-out MAE of entropy loss/R with this descriptor added must be below the 0.546 R baseline; if MAE is unchanged or worse, or the fitted sign corresponds to reduced entropy loss at small free paths, the hypothesis is rejected.

retained.name: window_size_mismatch
retained.hypothesis: Entropy loss grows with (i) the mismatch between periodic and probe-accessible limiting pore dimensions (narrow windows vs. larger cages create rotational traps) and (ii) the ratio of accessible surface area measures (geometric roughness of the confinement surface). The combined descriptor improves MAE of entropy loss/R beyond the baseline 14 inputs, with the largest gains for cage-window frameworks.
